extracted.intended_audience: readers and enthusiasts of maritime history, 19th-century shipping, and clipper-ship performance
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the qualities, performance, and historical record of mid-19th-century clipper and emigrant ships (design, construction, voyage times, accommodations, safety, and commercial outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mail contract delivery time and penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts requiring ships 'to land them in Australia in 68 days, or pay a penalty of £100 a day for every day over that time' (and an example of James Baines accepting 'to land the mails in 65 days with the same penalty attached').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an explicit contractual performance standard — timeliness measured in days with monetary penalties for delay; demonstrates the commercial pressure to shorten passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage speed and voyage-time records
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured performance in days land-to-land (e.g., Marco Polo: 68 days out to Port Phillip Heads; record passages such as 76 days, 69 land-to-land, round voyages in 5 months 21 days), and daily runs in miles (examples: best day 364 miles; four-day run 1344 miles; individual runs like 314, 332, 364 miles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary metric for evaluating a clipper's success; examples in the text (daily runs, knots, total days) are used to claim 'fastest ship in the world' status. Includes both individual best runs and aggregate voyage times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hull form and lines (design affecting speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporaneous technical appraisal: 'Her lines fore and aft are beautifully fine, her bearings are brought well down to the bilge; thus... she has an entrance as sharp as a steamboat and a run as clean as can be conceived... Below the draught line her bows are hollow; but above she swells out handsomely... with a bottom like a yacht, she has above water all the appearance of a frigate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hull geometry (fine ends, sharp entrance, clean run, balanced displacement) is presented as decisive for speed while retaining carrying capacity; quoted description serves as design-evaluation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship dimensions and tonnage
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative dimensions used to describe and evaluate vessels: length, beam, depth of hold, registered tonnage and burthen (examples: Marco Polo—length 185 ft, beam 38 ft, depth 30 ft, registered tonnage 1625, burthen over 2000; many other ships similarly listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic physical measures determine cargo/passenger capacity, stability, and seakeeping; often provided alongside performance figures to correlate size with speed or profitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction strength and timbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of build quality: 'Her timbering is enormous. Her deck beams are huge balks of pitch-pine. Her timbers are well formed and ponderous. The stem and stern frame are of the choicest material. The hanging and lodging knees are all natural crooks and are fitted to the greatest nicety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust framing, choice materials, and careful joinery are cited as indicators of seaworthiness and durability — important for long ocean voyages and heavy loading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passenger accommodations and ventilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Passenger-fit criteria: height between decks (8 feet), 'no pains have been spared in her construction to secure thorough ventilation', dining saloon details (maple, stained glass, ornamental pilasters), berths in separate staterooms, hatch-lights for cheerfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comfort, ventilation, and well-thought-out saloon/dormitory arrangements are presented as advances for emigrant travel and a selling point for passenger ships; used to evaluate suitability for long voyages with many emigrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-board medical provisions and mortality outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical provisioning and outcome measures: carrying a special hospital/sick bay and 'two doctors' and the resulting mortality report (on one voyage 'only two deaths of adults on board, both from natural causes, and only a few of children from measles' compared to typical 50–100 deaths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of surgeons/hospital and low mortality are used to evaluate the humane and practical quality of emigrant voyages; serves as evidence of superior arrangements for passenger safety and health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer selection and crew composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality and composition indicators: 'Her officers were chosen from the best ships sailing out of Liverpool', named officers, regular crew numbers (e.g., regular crew 30, plus 30 seamen working their passage), and instances of impressed/jailed crew for getting replacements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced officers and adequate crew complement are criteria for reliability and the ability to press the ship for fast passages; crew working their passage and officer provenance are signals of competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sail plan and sail-handling capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigging and sail equipment affecting performance: use of flying kites, three skysails on sliding gunter masts (man-of-war fashion), Cunningham's patent topsails, ability to reduce sail from royals to double reefs in 20 minutes, setting of stunsails, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex and effective sail plans plus quick sail-handling are evaluated as enabling higher sustained speeds and better control in varying conditions; text gives specific sail types and handling benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial cargo/specie capacity and profitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics of commercial success: carriage of specie and bullion safes, amounts of gold dust brought home (example: 'brought home £100,000 in gold dust'; specific voyages cleared profits like £8018 and £8920), freight received (e.g., $84,000), and advertised suitability for shippers of specie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volume and value of cargo (especially specie/gold dust), freight earned, and clear profit on voyages are used to evaluate a ship's commercial viability and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification, certificates and marketing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation and formal classification: A1 at Lloyd's designation; advertising copy ('The Splendid New Frigate-built Ship', 'THE FASTEST SHIP IN THE WORLD'); promotional notices touting speed and accommodations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification by Lloyd's and bold marketing claims serve as external validation and influence public perception and chartering; the text shows how advertisements use performance and fittings as selling points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ice hazard handling, damage resilience, and ability to jury-rig
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations of seaworthiness under ice conditions and post-damage performance: examples include Marco Polo tearing copper off her bow from small ice, Marco Polo colliding with an iceberg (bowsprit carried away, bow stove in, foremast sprung) and surviving by pumping and repair; detailed Indian Queen incident showing collision with iceberg, lost spars, jury-rigging (topmast secured to stump, topsail yards crossed on jury foremast), long drift to Valparaiso and final towing in by naval boats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ship's ability to withstand ice impact, perform emergency repairs (jury rigs), pump out water, and make for a port is a key safety/resilience criterion; narrative examples provide concrete behaviors to judge by.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable mishaps and reputational consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Relationship between accidents and professional reputation: e.g., Captain Forbes' 'eclipse' after the wreck of the Schomberg despite acquittal, leading to loss of standing and broken career; ship losses (Guiding Star lost with all hands) and their effect on lines/owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents at sea have long-term commercial and professional consequences; scrutiny of inquiry outcomes, public banquets/testimonials, and subsequent career arcs are used to evaluate the broader impact of mishaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage operational practices and captaincy style
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative captaincy criteria and operational choices: examples include Forbes' aggressive sail-carrying ('case of "Hell or Melbourne"'), disciplinary measures (padlocking sheets, clapping crew into prison to secure availability), starting voyages on 'lucky' days, and showmanship in banquets and public addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captain's seamanship, temperament, discipline methods, and publicity/charisma are presented as influential on performance and reputation — both constructive (record passages) and potentially damaging (public overpromises, later disgrace).
